title: Reynolds-number-dependent entrance bias in temperature polarization of lab-scale membrane distillation
authors: Soyoung Kim, Tiezheng Tong, Yinuo Noah Yao
abstract: Lab-scale membrane distillation (MD) modules are commonly used for membrane characterization and developing empirical heat-transfer correlations. Entrance-induced flow structures can introduce geometry-specific effects into measured temperature polarization (TP) and heat transfer. However, the dependence of these effects on module geometry and flow condition remains unclear. We performed three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of direct contact membrane distillation (DCMD) over inlet Reynolds numbers of $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}=10$-$1000$, focusing on side-chamber length and main-channel height. We discovered that counter-rotating streamwise vortices formed near the main-channel entrance across all geometries, but their downstream persistence increased with $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$. At lower $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$, the vortices mostly decayed before mid-channel, while at higher $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$ they persisted farther downstream and produced pronounced spatial variations in TP. Increasing side-chamber length reduced the secondary-flow kinetic energy entering the main channel, and generally strengthened TP, whereas increasing main-channel height reduced the bulk velocity and streamwise kinetic energy, resulting in a thicker thermal boundary layer and stronger TP. For most geometries, the deviation from the straight-channel baseline changed from stronger TP at lower $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$ to weaker TP at higher $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$. Entrance effects therefore vary in both magnitude and direction with operating condition and cannot be represented by a constant correction across the Reynolds-number range.

infographic.key_insight: Entrance-driven vortices in lab-scale DCMD cause Reynolds-number-dependent temperature polarization, and the bias can switch from stronger to weaker TP as flow rate increases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Membrane distillation correlations and module comparisons must account for entrance geometry and inlet Reynolds number, because a single correction factor will not capture heat-transfer bias across operating conditions.
method: 3D CFD of direct-contact membrane distillation modules
Swept inlet Reynolds number from 10 to 1000
Varied side-chamber length and main-channel height to isolate geometry effects
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports CFD results across multiple geometries and Reynolds numbers, showing vortex persistence, secondary-flow energy changes, and TP deviations relative to a straight-channel baseline.
infographic.watch_item: The findings are simulation-based, so transfer to real modules may depend on membrane properties, manufacturing tolerances, and experimental boundary conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Reynolds-number-dependent entrance bias in temperature polarization of lab-scale membrane distillation

title: High-fidelity Three-Dimensional Flow Field Reconstruction Driven by Turbulent Fluid Dynamics
authors: Hanlin Kong, Jianan Wei, Yuntian Chen, Yujia Wang, Wenguan Wang
abstract: High-fidelity three-dimensional turbulent flow fields are essential for scientific and engineering analyses, yet obtaining them through direct numerical simulation or high-resolution measurements remains expensive. Super-resolution reconstruction from coarse-grained data therefore offers a promising alternative, but remains fundamentally challenging because fine-scale structures are intrinsically three-dimensional and dynamically coupled across scales. Existing data-driven approaches still struggle to recover multiscale volumetric structures and their coherent temporal evolution. To address these limitations, we propose a turbulence-aware framework for time-resolved three-dimensional flow reconstruction. The framework couples a multiscale neural operator, designed to recover volumetric structures, with a state space model to promote temporal consistency in the reconstructed dynamics. In addition, Navier-Stokes residuals are incorporated as soft constraints to regularize the reconstruction toward physically plausible dynamics. A mixture-of-experts mechanism is also introduced to support unsupervised adaptation to unknown coarse-graining. Across evaluations on canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data, the proposed framework reduces reconstruction errors relative to learning-based and classical baselines, while better preserving multiscale spatial structure and coherent temporal evolution. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in reconstructing high-fidelity three-dimensional flow fields from coarse-grained data.

infographic.key_insight: A turbulence-aware model that combines multiscale volumetric reconstruction, temporal state-space modeling, and physics-based regularization can recover high-fidelity 3D turbulent flow fields from coarse data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables cheaper and more practical reconstruction of detailed flow fields for CFD analysis, visualization, and downstream engineering decision-making when full-resolution simulation or measurement is unavailable.
method: Multiscale neural operator reconstructs 3D spatial flow structures from coarse-grained inputs.
State space model enforces time-resolved consistency in the reconstructed dynamics.
Navier-Stokes residuals and a mixture-of-experts module add physics guidance and adaptation to unknown coarse-graining.
infographic.evidence_signal: The framework was evaluated on canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data, where it reduced reconstruction errors and better preserved multiscale structure and temporal coherence than learning-based and classical baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the quality of the physics residual formulation and the ability of the mixture-of-experts module to generalize to unseen coarse-graining patterns.
infographic.paper_title: High-fidelity Three-Dimensional Flow Field Reconstruction Driven by Turbulent Fluid Dynamics

title: Interaction of Sustained Vortex Shedding with a Phononic Subsurface: Effect of Positioning and Resonant Characteristics
authors: Sangwon Park, Vinod Ramakrishnan, Arturo Machado Burgos, Andres Goza, Kathryn H. Matlack
abstract: Phononic materials (PMs) have emerged as a promising candidate to passively and beneficially interact with unsteady flows. However, their fluid-structure interaction (FSI) with separated flows exhibiting sustained periodic vortex shedding remains completely unexplored. In this study, we use a high-fidelity immersed boundary method to investigate the strongly coupled, nonlinear FSI dynamics of vortex shedding from a fully separated flow over a flat plate, with an embedded PM subsurface (PSub) modeled as a grounded diatomic chain driving a compliant section on the flat plate. We probe the dependence of the coupled system dynamics on two parameters: (1) the PSub chordwise position, which sets its spatial relationship to the flow structure, and (2) the rate of growth of the resonant displacement amplitude of a PSub, a behavioral parameter identified as a key driving parameter in PSub interaction with latent vortex shedding in prior work. Simulation results show that these two parameters drive clear and systematic changes to the limit-cycle vortex shedding. The PSub chordwise position determines the limit cycle PM-FSI dynamics, which can be classified into four distinct regimes as a function of position, ranging from substantial amplification to strong attenuation of lift and drag oscillation amplitudes in the limit cycle. Results reveal a configuration that reduces lift oscillation amplitude by over 30% and drag oscillation amplitude by over 50% with less than 0.5% change in mean lift and drag. Displacement amplitude envelope primarily governs transient responsiveness toward the limit cycle, where its influence also depends on the chordwise position. We analyze characteristic frequencies, the phase relationship between PSub displacement and lift, and unsteady and mean flow fields of the vortex-shedding process to explain mechanisms by which the PM modifies the flow.

infographic.key_insight: A phononic subsurface embedded in a flat plate can passively reshape sustained vortex shedding, with its position and resonant growth rate tuning the flow between amplification and strong attenuation regimes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a passive control strategy for reducing unsteady lift and drag in separated-flow systems without materially changing mean aerodynamic loads.
method: High-fidelity immersed boundary simulations of fully separated flow over a flat plate with a compliant section driven by a grounded diatomic-chain phononic subsurface.
Parameter sweep over chordwise subsurface position and resonant displacement growth rate.
Analysis of limit-cycle behavior, lift/drag oscillations, phase relations, frequencies, and mean/unsteady flow fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulations identified four position-dependent limit-cycle regimes, including one case with over 30% lower lift oscillation and over 50% lower drag oscillation while mean lift and drag changed by less than 0.5%.
infographic.watch_item: The reported benefits are highly sensitive to subsurface placement and resonance characteristics, so performance may not generalize without careful design and flow-condition matching.
infographic.paper_title: Interaction of Sustained Vortex Shedding with a Phononic Subsurface: Effect of Positioning and Resonant Characteristics

title: Component-wise outer similarity of turbulent boundary layers with strong adverse-pressure gradient
authors: Yu-Xuan Shi, Mingze Ma, Xi Chen
abstract: The adverse-pressure-gradient (APG) effect challenges the classical scaling of turbulent boundary layers (TBLs) over a flat plate, and it remains unclear whether outer-layer similarity holds across a wide range of APG strengths.We assemble a benchmark comprising the present direct numerical simulation of a suction--blowing-induced separation bubble and published profiles, spanning Clauser parameters $β_e=0.04$--$180$ and Reynolds numbers $Re_θ=530$--$19000$. Across this broad $(β_e,Re_θ)$ parameter range, existing APG normalizations do not simultaneously collapse the two mean-velocity defects and four Reynolds-stress components, leaving open whether outer similarity persists. Instead of defining new scalings, we normalize each quantity by its value at a common location $y_s$. Results are shown using $y_s=0.5δ$, beyond the outer stress peaks. For each of the six quantities, the normalized profiles exhibit a common outer shape across the conditions, with collapse emerging for $y/δ\gtrsim0.2$ for the velocity defects and $y/δ\gtrsim0.4$ for the Reynolds stresses. The collapse-error analysis shows that outer self-similarity is retained over a broad range of $y_s$ within the outer region and is not restricted to $y_s=0.5δ$. Furthermore, explicit expressions are provided for the normalized outer profiles. These results support component-wise outer similarity under strong APGs and provide compact references for APG turbulence-model assessment and conditional profile reconstruction.

infographic.key_insight: Even under very strong adverse-pressure gradients, the outer region of turbulent boundary layers shows component-wise self-similarity when each mean-defect or Reynolds-stress profile is normalized by its value at a common outer location.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides compact reference profiles for assessing turbulence models and reconstructing APG boundary-layer statistics without needing a single universal scaling law.
method: Compiled a benchmark from new DNS of a suction--blowing separation bubble plus published APG/TBL data.
Covered a wide range of Clauser parameters and Reynolds numbers, then normalized six quantities by their value at a chosen outer reference height $y_s$ (shown with $y_s=0.5\delta$).
Tested collapse across two mean-velocity defects and four Reynolds-stress components and quantified outer self-similarity via collapse-error analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark spans $\beta_e=0.04$--$180$ and $Re_\theta=530$--$19000$, and the abstract reports consistent outer-shape collapse for all six quantities, with velocity defects collapsing for $y/\delta\gtrsim0.2$ and stresses for $y/\delta\gtrsim0.4$.
infographic.watch_item: The observed similarity is component-wise and depends on choosing an outer-region reference location, so it should not be interpreted as a universal single-scaling collapse for the entire boundary layer.
infographic.paper_title: Component-wise outer similarity of turbulent boundary layers with strong adverse-pressure gradient

title: Hurricane Laura-induced loads on wind turbines -- Part I: High-fidelity modeling and sensitivity to turbulent inflow conditions
authors: Miguel Sanchez-Gomez, Lucas Carmo, Matthew Churchfield, Jason Jonkman, Walter Musial
abstract: Tropical cyclones can produce extreme winds in the lowest portion of the boundary layer, posing high risks to critical energy infrastructure, including wind energy systems. This study evaluates the dynamic response of an idling wind turbine to turbulent inflow generated during the passage of a hurricane. We performed large-eddy simulations of Hurricane Laura (2020) at several grid resolutions -- coarse $(Δx=55.55\,{\rm m})$, intermediate $(Δx=25\,{\rm m})$, and fine $(Δx=10\,{\rm m})$ -- to investigate differences in mean flow characteristics and turbulence structures as the hurricane progresses across a virtual wind turbine location. The large-eddy simulation data served as direct inflow conditions for aeroelastic simulations to assess the turbine's response. Our results reveal significant differences in the mean wind and turbulent flow structures between the grid resolutions, leading to distinct impacts on the wind turbine's aeroelastic behavior. These findings emphasize the need for high-resolution inflow information to better predict extreme loads and inform the design of wind turbines in regions frequently affected by tropical cyclones. As a continuation of this work, Part II of this study will evaluate the turbine's response from different locations relative to the storm's trajectory and compare it with current wind turbine design practices.

infographic.key_insight: High-resolution hurricane LES shows that grid-dependent differences in mean wind and turbulence can materially change the aeroelastic loads seen by an idling wind turbine.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accurate extreme-load design for turbines in tropical-cyclone regions requires high-fidelity inflow fields, not just coarse storm-scale wind estimates.
method: Large-eddy simulations of Hurricane Laura were run at three grid resolutions: 55.55 m, 25 m, and 10 m.
LES outputs were used directly as inflow for aeroelastic wind-turbine simulations.
The turbine response was evaluated as the hurricane passed a virtual turbine location.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports significant differences in mean wind and turbulent structures across the three LES resolutions, producing distinct turbine aeroelastic responses.
infographic.watch_item: Results are based on a virtual location and one storm case, so broader design guidance should be validated across more tracks, intensities, and turbine states.
infographic.paper_title: Hurricane Laura-induced loads on wind turbines -- Part I: High-fidelity modeling and sensitivity to turbulent inflow conditions

title: Some generalizations of the tornado model
authors: S. N. Artekha
abstract: A possible mechanism of tornado generation is associated with the Schwarzschild criterion for convective instability. The supercooled cloud-air mixture near the axis starts to descend and, due to the super adiabatic temperature gradient, the overheated near-surface air mass rises. The complete system of equations for full model includes equations for the stream function, for the azimuthal velocity component, and for the change in density. The refined model considers rotating convection within the framework of ideal hydrodynamics. The simplest model uses a separate equation for the stream function and can be applied to the initial stage of vortex generation. Within the framework of the simplest model, an analytical solution is combined from 8 linear dependencies by height. Rotation increases due to the conservation of angular momentum. Within the framework of the refined model, some unidirectional differential rotation arises, but it depends on boundary conditions (can be local). The full model studies the tornado development as rotating convection from the very beginning to the quasi-stationary stage. Velocity components increase in a coordinated manner. Two cases are considered: a single whirlwind and a two-eyed tornado. Radial flows converge towards the central part of the tornado near the earth surface, and there is an outflow from the "wall" to the axis and to the periphery near the top of the tornado. The maximum vertical velocity component is achieved at a certain radial distance at a certain height. The maximum azimuthal velocity component is achieved in the tornado "wall". Tornado generation criteria are discussed.

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that tornadoes can be modeled as rotating convection driven by convective instability, with vortex intensification governed by angular-momentum conservation and boundary-dependent differential rotation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a staged hydrodynamic framework for predicting tornado initiation and evolution, useful for simplified vortex modeling and for comparing single-core versus two-eyes tornado structures.
method: Formulates a full hydrodynamic model with equations for stream function, azimuthal velocity, and density change.
Develops a refined ideal-hydrodynamics model for rotating convection and a simplest model for early vortex formation.
Analyzes flow structure, including radial inflow near the surface, outflow aloft, and peak azimuthal/vertical velocity locations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical solutions and theoretical criteria across three model levels, but does not mention experiments or numerical validation.
infographic.watch_item: The strongest differential-rotation effects depend on boundary conditions, so predictions may be highly model- and setup-sensitive.
infographic.paper_title: Some generalizations of the tornado model

title: Effect of leading edge geometry on aerodynamic performance of a flat plate
authors: Intesaaf Ashraf, Hamid Hassan Khan, Majid Hassan Khan
abstract: Flow separation around flat plate is influenced by the thickness and leading edge geometry, which creates the shear stresses and pressure distribution manifesting into unsteady aerodynamic forces. Leading edge geometries have been widely reported but the influence of leading edge curvature at low Reynolds numbers (Re) have found less attention. The present study uses two dimensional numerical simulation to investigate the effect of a hemispherical curvature (protuberance) at the leading edge and reports how vortex shedding, shedding frequencies and aerodynamic forces are affected over a range of angles of attack ($0^\circ \leq α\leq 25^\circ$) at Re = 1000. Thicker vortical regions are formed near the plate with curvature at the leading edge. Onset of shedding is noted at angle of attack of $5^\circ$ for the plate with curvature at the leading edge and it gets delayed for simple flat plate. The temporal force coefficients on the plates show multiple frequencies at higher angles of attack. The plate with curvature at the leading edge has a glide ratio of 1 at $0^\circ$ angle of attack and has equivalent glide ratio to that of simple flat plate at higher angles of attack. The simple flat plate has better glide ratios at moderate angles of attack like $5^\circ, 10^\circ$ and $15^\circ$. The results will help in making engineering informed design decisions for smaller unmanned aerial/aquatic vehicles cruising at low Reynolds numbers.

infographic.key_insight: At Re = 1000, adding a hemispherical leading-edge curvature changes separation and vortex shedding, producing thicker vortical regions and earlier shedding onset than a simple flat plate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Leading-edge geometry can be tuned to trade off glide ratio and unsteady loading for low-Re small UAV or aquatic vehicle design.
method: 2D numerical simulations
Angle of attack sweep from 0° to 25°
Comparison of simple flat plate vs. plate with hemispherical leading-edge curvature at Re = 1000
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports changes in shedding onset, shedding frequencies, force-coefficient spectra, and glide ratio across angles of attack, with the curved plate showing onset at 5° and multiple force frequencies at higher angles.
infographic.watch_item: Results are based on 2D simulations at a single Reynolds number, so 3D effects and broader operating conditions may limit direct transfer to real hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Effect of leading edge geometry on aerodynamic performance of a flat plate

title: Extreme-Scale Super-Resolution of Homogeneous Turbulence from a Single Realization
authors: Arth Sojitra, Muhammad Abid, Omer San
abstract: Homogeneous turbulent flows exhibit recurring multiscale structures across spatially separated regions, suggesting that a single flow realization may contain sufficient information to learn representations of unresolved scales. We investigate this hypothesis through an extreme super-resolution framework in which a wide-activation deep super-resolution (WDSR) network is trained exclusively on overlapping patches extracted from a single high-resolution turbulent realization. Previously unseen flow fields are reconstructed through patchwise prediction followed by Hann-window-weighted overlap-add assembly. The framework is evaluated for two-dimensional homogeneous isotropic turbulence at super-resolution factors of x32 and x64, representing severe spatial under-resolution. Despite the limited training data, the proposed approach reconstructs coherent vortical structures and recovers fine-scale features more accurately than conventional interpolation. Spectral and statistical analyses further demonstrate improved recovery of high-wavenumber energy content and multiscale flow characteristics. To assess the effectiveness of exploiting internal spatial information, we compare the proposed framework against WDSR models trained on 1, 25, 50, and 100 complete high-resolution snapshots without patch extraction. This comparison distinguishes the benefits of localized learning from those associated with increasing the number of training realizations. The results demonstrate that exploiting spatial redundancy within a single turbulent realization enables accurate reconstruction of previously unseen flow fields, even under extreme spatial under-resolution. These findings establish single-realization patch-based learning as a promising data-efficient approach for turbulent super-resolution when high-resolution training data are scarce.

infographic.key_insight: A single high-resolution turbulent realization contains enough recurring multiscale structure to train a patch-based super-resolution model that reconstructs unseen flow fields with high fidelity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a data-efficient path for recovering fine-scale turbulence features when high-resolution simulation or measurement data are scarce.
method: Train a WDSR network only on overlapping patches from one high-resolution 2D homogeneous isotropic turbulence snapshot.
Predict super-resolved patches for unseen fields and stitch them with Hann-window-weighted overlap-add.
Benchmark against interpolation and WDSR models trained on 1, 25, 50, and 100 full snapshots.
infographic.evidence_signal: At x32 and x64 super-resolution, the method recovers coherent vortices and improves high-wavenumber energy and multiscale statistics relative to conventional interpolation.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on spatial stationarity and patch overlap quality, so results may not transfer directly to non-homogeneous or transient flows without retraining.
infographic.paper_title: Extreme-Scale Super-Resolution of Homogeneous Turbulence from a Single Realization

title: eMOOD: Entropy-Based Multidimensional Optimal Order Detection for High-Order Shock-Capturing Finite-Volume Schemes
authors: Michał Umiński, Panagiotis Tsoutsanis, Ahmed A Sheikh Al-Shabab, Alan S. Dawes
abstract: We present eMOOD, an entropy-guided evolution of the Multidimensional Optimal Order Detection (MOOD) framework for high-order finite-volume methods on unstructured meshes. A novel troubled-cell indicator based on numerical entropy production replaces the classical relaxed discrete maximum principle. Using entropy generation as a physically motivated measure of non-smoothness, the detector targets shocks, contact discontinuities and under-resolved flow features with a compact stencil. Compared with conventional MOOD detection, eMOOD reduces flagged cells by up to 75%, improving efficiency and reducing memory-access overhead. The detector is used within both the classical MOOD cascade of progressively reduced-order schemes and a novel MOOD-CWENO hybrid, which retains inexpensive linear reconstruction in smooth regions and activates nonlinear high-order reconstruction only where needed. Implemented in the open-source parallel solver UCNS3D, the methodology is assessed on the Shu-Osher shock-entropy-wave interaction, double Mach reflection, supersonic forward-facing step, shock-helium-bubble interaction and triple material point problems. These benchmarks encompass strong shock interactions, shock-induced instabilities, multi-material interfaces and vortex-dominated flows, testing robustness, shock capturing and accuracy on unstructured meshes. Results show that eMOOD preserves the accuracy and robustness of reference CWENO and MOOD formulations while achieving speed-ups of up to 20% without loss of solution quality. Its compact detection stencil, reduced memory footprint and improved localisation offer a more scalable and efficient framework for massively parallel high-order compressible-flow simulations. infographic.key_insight: eMOOD replaces MOOD’s relaxed maximum-principle detector with an entropy-based troubled-cell indicator that flags non-smooth regions more selectively, enabling efficient shock capturing on unstructured meshes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes high-order finite-volume solvers for compressible multiphase flows faster and more scalable by reducing unnecessary limiter activation, memory traffic, and reconstruction cost.
method: Uses numerical entropy production as a compact-stencil troubled-cell detector.
Integrates the detector into both classical MOOD cascades and a MOOD-CWENO hybrid.
Deploys in UCNS3D for unstructured-mesh, parallel shock-capturing simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across Shu-Osher, double Mach reflection, forward-facing step, shock-helium-bubble, and triple-material-point benchmarks, the method reduced flagged cells by up to 75% and delivered speed-ups of up to 20% while preserving solution quality.
infographic.watch_item: Entropy-based detection must be tuned carefully for complex flows, since overly aggressive or overly conservative thresholds could misclassify weak gradients or under-resolved interfaces.
infographic.paper_title: eMOOD: Entropy-Based Multidimensional Optimal Order Detection for High-Order Shock-Capturing Finite-Volume Schemes

title: Two-Way Coupled Dynamics of Quantized Vortex Bundle Formation in Spatially Periodic Normal-Fluid Turbulence
authors: Hiromichi Kobayashi, Makoto Tsubota, Rio Yokota
abstract: Using fully coupled two-way simulations combining the vortex filament model with the Navier--Stokes equations, we discover that quantized vortices in superfluid $^4$He are systematically rolled up into coherent bundles within normal-fluid vortex tubes. Although co-rotating quantized vortices do not aggregate spontaneously, mutual friction with the normal fluid actively drives their bundling, directly inheriting the spatial hierarchy of classical turbulence. Mutual friction excites high-wavenumber normal-fluid vortex tubes adjacent to quantized vortices, while the superfluid forms a nested structure of thick low-wavenumber outer tubes and fine high-wavenumber inner tubes around the vortex lines. A distinct time lag between superfluid kinetic energy and dissipation fuels the energy cascade, giving rise to Kolmogorov's $k^{-5/3}$ spectrum. Crucially, bundle lifetimes are governed by the ratio of the local coupling time scale $t_\mathrm{cl}$ to the Kolmogorov dissipation time scale $τ_η$ ($t_\mathrm{cl}/τ_η< 20$), leading to enhanced thermal stability at higher temperatures. These findings establish a unified mechanism for two-fluid multiscale vortex organization.

infographic.key_insight: Two-way coupling between superfluid vortices and normal-fluid turbulence actively rolls quantized vortices into coherent bundles, reproducing a classical-like multiscale hierarchy and a Kolmogorov energy cascade.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result clarifies how heat transfer, dissipation, and vortex organization in superfluid helium can be predicted and potentially controlled by accounting for mutual friction and two-fluid coupling.
method: Fully coupled vortex filament and Navier–Stokes simulations
Spatially periodic normal-fluid turbulence with mutual friction feedback
Comparison of vortex structure, spectra, and time scales across temperatures
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports direct simulation evidence of bundle formation, a k^-5/3 spectrum, and a coupling-time-to-dissipation-time threshold t_cl/τ_eta < 20 associated with stable bundles.
infographic.watch_item: The mechanism is demonstrated in a periodic simulation setting, so real-flow geometry, forcing details, and parameter ranges may limit immediate transferability.
infographic.paper_title: Two-Way Coupled Dynamics of Quantized Vortex Bundle Formation in Spatially Periodic Normal-Fluid Turbulence

title: Partially-Averaged Navier-Stokes simulation of turbulent annular Poiseulle flow
authors: Li-Toong Yap, Marten Klein, Heiko Schmidt
abstract: Turbulent annular Poiseulle flow is commonly encountered in various engineering applications, such as heat exchangers. The effects of the inner wall transverse curvature on the flowfield, characterised by the ratio of inner and outer radii $η= R_{i}/R_{o}$, have been studied previously using Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS). Scale-resolving simulations based on a Reynolds-Averaged Navier Stokes framework offer a potentially cheaper alternative to traditional Large Eddy Simulations (LES); however it is not clear if such models are able to capture the turbulence anisotropy in the turbulent annular pipe flow. In the present study, turbulent annular Poiseulle flow at $Re_{D_{h}} = 8900$ is performed with the Partially-Averaged Navier Stokes (PANS) model, a variable-resolution turbulence model that is based on the conventional RANS modelling. The ability of the PANS model to capture the effects of the transverse wall curvature is found to be comparable with DNS and other RANS-based scale-resolving approaches despite its relative simplicity and reduced computational cost.

infographic.key_insight: A Partially-Averaged Navier-Stokes (PANS) model can reproduce the curvature-driven turbulence behavior in annular Poiseuille flow with accuracy comparable to DNS and other scale-resolving RANS-based methods.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a lower-cost option for predicting turbulent flow in curved annular passages relevant to heat exchangers and similar engineering systems.
method: Simulated turbulent annular Poiseuille flow at Re_Dh = 8900.
Used the PANS variable-resolution turbulence framework built on conventional RANS modeling.
Assessed the influence of inner-wall transverse curvature via the radius ratio η = Ri/Ro.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the PANS results capture transverse wall curvature effects comparably to DNS and other RANS-based scale-resolving approaches.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on model resolution settings and careful calibration, so the reduced-cost advantage should be validated for other geometries and Reynolds numbers.
infographic.paper_title: Partially-Averaged Navier-Stokes simulation of turbulent annular Poiseulle flow

title: Ambient-pressure effects on shock emission and liquid-shell expansion following optical breakdown inside water droplets
authors: M. Brugge, S. van Belois, S. S. Ade, O. O. Versolato, M. Kharbedia
abstract: We experimentally investigate the deformation and breakup of micrometer-sized water droplets following nanosecond laser-induced breakdown in the finite-beam regime D0/Db~2 and over a range of ambient pressures. Simultaneous measurements of the liquid deformation and emitted shock wave enable the gas and liquid phase dynamics to be distinguished quantitatively. Under fixed external focusing conditions, the curved droplet interface focuses and internally reflects the incident light, leading to transient plasma formation within the liquid and generating the pressure load that drives droplet deformation. At low laser energies (El<1mJ), plasma formation localized near the rear droplet-air interface produces an interfacial bubble that expands into a thin liquid film susceptible to hydrodynamic instabilities and ultimately collapses under the action of surface tension. The internal pressure is partially released into the surrounding air, generating a propagating shock wave. At higher energies (El>1mJ), the droplet is ablated along the laser axis, resulting in the explosive formation of a liquid shell and multiple shock fronts, both exhibiting supersonic expansion velocities. While the shock wave dynamics are well described within the framework of strong blast wave theory, we show that the shell expansion can be understood as being driven by the pressure load generated during plasma expansion inside the droplet. Consequently, the droplet expands as a liquid shell that subsequently follows ballistic motion and ultimately undergoes complete atomization. Although changing surrounding gas density substantially alters the propagation of the emitted shock wave, the droplet morphology and expansion dynamics remain nearly unchanged, given the internal load of the plasma-driven pressure.

infographic.key_insight: Laser breakdown inside a water droplet generates an internal plasma pressure load that drives liquid-shell expansion and breakup, while the emitted shock wave is strongly affected by ambient pressure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results help predict and control droplet atomization and shock emission in laser-based spray, microfluidic, and laser-processing applications.
method: Nanosecond laser-induced breakdown was performed inside micrometer-sized water droplets in the finite-beam regime (D0/Db≈2).
Simultaneous imaging of droplet deformation and shock-wave propagation was used to separate liquid and gas-phase dynamics.
Experiments were repeated over a range of ambient pressures and laser energies to compare low-energy bubble-driven deformation with high-energy shell ablation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports simultaneous quantitative measurements showing that shock propagation changes substantially with ambient pressure, while droplet morphology and expansion remain nearly unchanged under the same internal plasma-driven load.
infographic.watch_item: The mechanism is established for a specific droplet size and finite-beam focusing condition, so extrapolation to other droplet sizes, beam geometries, or liquids should be done cautiously.
infographic.paper_title: Ambient-pressure effects on shock emission and liquid-shell expansion following optical breakdown inside water droplets

title: Numerical Modeling of a Metallic Alloy Droplet Impact, Solidification, and Macrosegregation
authors: Ehsan Amani, Ali Moinirad
abstract: For the first time, we study the effects of mass transfer on alloy droplet impact, solidification, and solute non-homogeneity or MacroSegregation (MS). For this purpose, a multi-physics model, including fully-coupled hydrodynamics of multiphase flow, wetting, conjugate heat transfer, phase change, and mass transfer, is established and validated carefully across several benchmarks. In addition, a concentration-flux-correction algorithm is proposed to conserve the solute mass within the droplet at the numerical discretization level. The validated model is subsequently used to explore the impact and solidification of an alloy droplet. The results show that accounting for mass transfer and solute transport improves the prediction of the dynamics of a solidifying splat, in a consistent manner with experimental observations, while this effect has been neglected in all previous studies. The analysis demonstrates that this improvement results from the flow sensitivity to the mushy region thickness, which is regulated by local solute concentration through the solidus and liquidus temperatures. Furthermore, analyses of the MS map identify several critical segregation regions most susceptible to defect initiation, such as cracking, including a long negatively segregated vein within the lamella, formed by the severe advective flow through the mush in the middle stages of the impact, a positively segregated region near the rim of the splat, appearing as a result of hook formation, and a major positively segregated zone at the top of the rim, which develops following the accumulation of the solute-rich melt sustained by washout from the lamella.

infographic.key_insight: Including solute mass transfer in droplet impact and solidification changes the predicted flow, mushy-zone evolution, and macrosegregation patterns in ways that better match experiments.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model improves prediction of solidifying alloy splat shape and defect-prone segregation zones, which is important for additive manufacturing, thermal spray, and casting processes.
method: Fully coupled multiphysics solver for multiphase hydrodynamics, wetting, heat transfer, phase change, and solute transport
Concentration-flux-correction algorithm to enforce solute mass conservation at the discretization level
Validation against several benchmarks before simulating alloy droplet impact and solidification
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports careful validation across several benchmarks and improved agreement with experimental observations when mass transfer is included.
infographic.watch_item: The approach adds model and numerical complexity, so accurate prediction depends on robust treatment of mushy-zone properties and solute-conservation enforcement.
infographic.paper_title: Numerical Modeling of a Metallic Alloy Droplet Impact, Solidification, and Macrosegregation

title: Active Sculpting: morphodynamics of internally stirred active vesicles
authors: Devadevan M M, Brato Chakrabarti
abstract: Active flows are often confined by soft, deformable boundaries that they can push against, reshape, and in turn get reorganized by. Motivated by this interplay, we combine theory and numerical simulations to analyze the morphodynamics of an elastic vesicle enclosing a dilute suspension of extensile active particles. We model the two-dimensional vesicle as a weakly extensible elastic ring with bending rigidity, immersed in a Stokesian fluid, and describe the confined active suspension using a kinetic theory. The vesicle and the suspension are coupled hydrodynamically, through the kinematic and dynamic boundary conditions at the interface, and energetically, through a single alignment interaction that simultaneously aligns active particles with the membrane and the membrane with the particles. We show that this interaction reduces to a weak-anchoring boundary condition familiar from passive liquid crystals and derive a closed-form quiescent equilibrium state in which the nematic order in the suspension organizes into a vortex with a +1 defect core. A stability analysis of this state predicts an ordered hierarchy of activity thresholds at which successive shape modes of the vesicle are destabilized, as well as a purely passive, anchoring-driven instability of floppy vesicles. Nonlinear simulations, performed with a volume-conserving immersed boundary method, reveal that each threshold crossing gives rise to a distinct emergent state: a static spindle with boundary-pinned defects, a rotor that tank treads against its own rotation, a fluctuating spinner, and a turbulent state in which the vesicle acts as a self-stirring compartment. Beyond demonstrating how boundary deformability sculpts, and is sculpted by, confined active matter, our results open the door to study hydrodynamic interactions between such active vesicles and to use membrane fluctuations as a probe of activity of suspensions.

infographic.key_insight: An active particle suspension inside an elastic vesicle can self-organize the membrane into a sequence of distinct morphodynamic states, from stable vortical order to spinning, fluctuating, and turbulent shapes as activity increases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work shows how soft boundary design and anchoring interactions can be used to control, diagnose, or harness active flows in deformable microcapsules and bioinspired soft devices.
method: 2D weakly extensible elastic-ring model with bending rigidity
Kinetic-theory description of confined dilute extensile active particles
Hydrodynamic and energetic coupling solved with stability analysis plus immersed-boundary nonlinear simulations
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical stability thresholds and nonlinear simulation results that identify a hierarchy of shape instabilities and resulting emergent states.
infographic.watch_item: The model is two-dimensional and idealized, so quantitative transfer to real 3D vesicles may require care in calibration of anchoring strength, extensibility, and active-particle parameters.
infographic.paper_title: Active Sculpting: morphodynamics of internally stirred active vesicles

title: Response of Confined Mesoscale Flames to Acoustic Forcing
authors: Akhil Aravind, Balasundaram Mohan, Saptarshi Basu
abstract: Mesoscale combustion plays a vital role in applications ranging from portable power generation to micro-propulsion systems. This study investigates the response of mesoscale flames to upstream acoustic forcing across three characteristic flame regimes: Flames with Repetitive Extinction and Ignition (FREI), Stable Flames (SF), and Propagating Flames (PF). Acoustic forcing is applied over a broad range of pressure intensities at the first harmonic of the combustor tube. At low forcing intensities, all the flame regimes exhibit oscillations at the forcing frequency without qualitative changes in their respective flame behaviours. However, as the acoustic pressure increases, all flame regimes transition to a common unsteady regime characterised by periodic ignition-extinction cycles (resembling FREI) alongside strong oscillations at the forcing frequency. This response is identified as the oscillating FREI (O-FREI) regime, in which increasing forcing intensity leads to a reduction in the mean heat release rate, an amplification of oscillations at the forcing frequency, and a drop in the Strouhal number associated with the ignition-extinction cycle. The response characteristics across all flame regimes are examined in detail and are further complemented using reduced-order mathematical models.

infographic.key_insight: Acoustic forcing can drive very different mesoscale flame regimes into a shared oscillatory ignition-extinction state (O-FREI), with stronger forcing reducing mean heat release while amplifying forcing-frequency oscillations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding how confinement and acoustic forcing destabilize mesoscale flames helps design more robust micro-combustors and portable power systems that must operate under unsteady flow conditions.
method: Applied upstream acoustic forcing at the combustor’s first harmonic across a wide range of pressure intensities.
Compared three flame regimes: FREI, stable flames, and propagating flames.
Used reduced-order mathematical models to interpret the observed transitions and oscillation dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports regime-dependent responses that converge to O-FREI at higher forcing, including lower mean heat release, stronger forcing-frequency oscillations, and reduced Strouhal number for ignition-extinction cycles.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions are based on a confined mesoscale combustor and first-harmonic forcing, so the observed transition may not generalize directly to other geometries, fuels, or forcing spectra.
infographic.paper_title: Response of Confined Mesoscale Flames to Acoustic Forcing

title: Pumping by Two-frequency Steady Streaming: Impact of Amplitude Ratio and Phase
authors: Hyun S. Lee, Becca Thomases, William D. Ristenpart, Robert D. Guy
abstract: The classical phenomenon of steady streaming around a circular cylinder oscillating with a single frequency results in a symmetric quadrupole-like flow structure. In [H.S.\ Lee, \textit{et al.}, J.\ Fluid Mech.\ 1038, A34 (2026)], we demonstrated using asymptotic analysis and numerical simulations that a cylinder vibrating with two frequencies yields asymmetrical steady streaming that pumps the fluid in one direction. The asymptotic expansion at small amplitude showed that pumping occurs at third order or higher depending on the frequency ratio, but the solutions are analytically intractable and the influence of key control parameters, like the amplitude ratio and phase difference, remained undetermined. Here, we analyze two-frequency steady streaming on an annular domain and reduce the equations from the asymptotic expansion to a series of boundary value problems of one spatial dimension, which can be numerically solved efficiently. For frequency ratio 2, we show that the net force on the cylinder is proportional to $\cos(φ- φ^*(\text{Re}))β/ (1+β^2)^{3/2}$, where $β$ is the amplitude ratio, $φ$ is the phase difference, Re is the Reynolds number, and $φ^*(\text{Re})$ is the phase that gives the largest force. To test whether the force on an enclosed annulus serves as a useful proxy for pumping in an open system, we also performed numerical simulations of a cylinder oscillating with two-frequencies in a rectangular channel. Our computations demonstrate that the net flux through the channel is directly proportional to the net force on the annulus over all parameter ranges tested. Finally, we discuss the implications for using two-frequency oscillations to pump fluid in lab-on-a-chip and other devices.

infographic.key_insight: Two-frequency cylinder oscillations create controllable asymmetric steady streaming, and the resulting pumping strength depends strongly on the amplitude ratio and phase difference.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a tunable mechanism for microfluidic pumping in lab-on-a-chip devices, with force on an annulus serving as a practical proxy for net channel flux.
method: Reduced the asymptotic steady-streaming equations to a sequence of 1D boundary value problems on an annulus.
Solved these problems numerically to map how force varies with amplitude ratio, phase, and Reynolds number.
Validated the annulus proxy by comparing with direct simulations in a rectangular channel.
infographic.evidence_signal: For frequency ratio 2, the net force follows a closed-form dependence on phase and amplitude ratio, and channel simulations show net flux is directly proportional to annulus force across the tested parameter ranges.
infographic.watch_item: The force-to-flux proxy was tested only over the simulated parameter range, so device design should verify scaling before relying on it in new geometries or extreme operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Pumping by Two-frequency Steady Streaming: Impact of Amplitude Ratio and Phase

title: PANDA-D: Interface-free determination of two dynamic contact angles
authors: Georgii K. Vandyshev, Grigorii S. Gorkaev, Nikolay D. Kondratyuk, Kirill M. Gerke, Ilia V. Kopanichuk
abstract: Contact angles are central descriptors of wetting and capillary behavior at solid--fluid interfaces. Dynamic contact angles in molecular simulations are commonly extracted from two-dimensional liquid--vapor contours and near-wall tangent fits. We introduce PANDA-D, an extension of Predicting Angle from Nanoscale Density Analysis (PANDA) that determines both contact angles of a driven liquid roll without extracting an interface. The density profile measures occupied layer width but does not identify which meniscus is advancing. The method resolves this ambiguity by jointly fitting density and the layerwise center-of-mass displacement relative to the roll. A circular-meniscus model maps these profiles to receding and advancing angles and an effective near-wall offset. On synthetic rolls with prescribed angles, the reconstruction error is $0.29^\circ$ root-mean-square. We then analyze force-driven Lennard--Jones rolls between crystalline walls. Joint fits reproduce both measured profiles, whereas density-only fits can match density while assigning incorrect asymmetry. The resulting angles agree with independently determined circle-fit angles to $0.84^\circ$ root-mean-square. Across four wall--fluid attractions, the receding angle decreases and the advancing angle increases with force, approximately linearly over the studied ranges. By eliminating contour thresholds and near-wall tangent extrapolation from the primary estimate, the two-profile approach enables reproducible, automated angle analysis across molecular trajectories.

infographic.key_insight: PANDA-D infers both advancing and receding dynamic contact angles directly from density and center-of-mass profiles, avoiding explicit interface extraction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more reproducible, automated wetting analysis in molecular simulations where contour-based angle estimation can be threshold-sensitive and ambiguous.
method: Fits a circular-meniscus model to the liquid roll using two observables: density profile and layerwise center-of-mass displacement.
Disambiguates which meniscus is advancing by jointly constraining both profiles.
Returns receding angle, advancing angle, and an effective near-wall offset without contour tracing.
infographic.evidence_signal: On synthetic rolls, the method achieved 0.29° RMS reconstruction error, and on Lennard-Jones rolls it matched independent circle-fit angles within 0.84° RMS.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on the validity of the circular-meniscus assumption and the quality of the layerwise density/displacement profiles, especially near the wall.
infographic.paper_title: PANDA-D: Interface-free determination of two dynamic contact angles

title: Wave-driven geostrophic vortices in rotating turbulence
authors: Vladimir Parfenyev, Sergey Vergeles
abstract: We perform direct numerical simulations of rotating turbulence to investigate the mechanisms responsible for the maintenance of large-scale geostrophic vortices. We confirm that the Reynolds stresses generated by inertial waves are consistent with the Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes balance of the large-scale flow and demonstrate the predicted cyclone-anticyclone asymmetry, with cyclones exhibiting stronger azimuthal velocities and more compact cores. Wave-field analysis provides evidence that geostrophic vortices selectively reflect and absorb inertial waves according to the sign of their angular momentum. Wave absorption occurs either through the formation of a critical layer ahead of the reflection point or through enhanced viscous dissipation associated with increasing local wavenumber. As rotation increases, fewer inertial waves undergo resonant absorption, reducing angular-momentum transfer to the vortices and weakening the geostrophic flow. Consequently, the fraction of energy contained in geostrophic modes depends non-monotonically on the rotation rate, demonstrating that sufficiently rapid rotation can ultimately suppress, rather than enhance, turbulence two-dimensionalization.

infographic.key_insight: In rotating turbulence, geostrophic vortices are sustained by inertial-wave Reynolds stresses, with cyclones growing stronger and more compact than anticyclones, while very rapid rotation can reduce rather than enhance two-dimensionalization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results help predict how rotation controls large-scale coherent vortices and angular-momentum transport in geophysical and rotating-engineering flows.
method: Direct numerical simulations of rotating turbulence
Wave-field analysis of inertial-wave/vortex interactions
Comparison with Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes balance for large-scale flow
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports simulated flow data showing Reynolds-stress consistency with RANS balance, cyclone-anticyclone asymmetry, and a non-monotonic fraction of geostrophic energy versus rotation rate.
infographic.watch_item: The absorption and vortex-strength trends may depend on rotation regime and model resolution, so extrapolation to other forcing conditions or higher Reynolds numbers should be done carefully.
infographic.paper_title: Wave-driven geostrophic vortices in rotating turbulence

title: Preferential concentration in a periodically forced particle-laden turbulent planar jet
authors: Mohammad Ahmad, Pierre Bragança, Christophe Cuvier, Martin Obligado
abstract: Periodic forcing is common in particle-laden jets, yet its influence on turbulence and inertial-particle clustering remains poorly understood. We investigate a turbulent planar jet at two Reynolds numbers, approximately 4950 and 9900 based on nozzle height, subjected to sinusoidal forcing at a frequency three orders of magnitude below the preferred jet instability. Hot-wire anemometry and high-speed particle imaging characterise the carrier turbulence, while Voronoi tessellations quantify preferential concentration of dilute inertial droplets. Despite its low frequency and moderate amplitude, forcing substantially modifies turbulence while leaving the mean-flow development nearly unchanged. The integral scale decreases by up to $40\%$, while forced and unforced jets retain the same time-averaged relationship between the dimensionless dissipation coefficient and Taylor-scale Reynolds number. Within the forcing cycle, velocity fluctuations and the Taylor microscale vary approximately in opposite phase, keeping the Taylor-scale Reynolds number within $\pm10\%$ of its cycle mean despite substantial variations in dissipation and Kolmogorov time scale. Particle clustering is even more sensitive, with forcing increasing mean preferential concentration and producing phase-dependent variations of $21$--$49\%$ of the cycle mean. Clustering peaks when the Kolmogorov time scale is largest, corresponding to the smallest particle Stokes number. Thus, markedly different clustering states occur at similar instantaneous Taylor-scale Reynolds numbers. These findings demonstrate that weak temporal modulation can control particle organisation without substantially altering the mean transporting flow.

infographic.key_insight: A weak, low-frequency forcing barely changes the jet’s mean development but strongly alters turbulence scales and boosts inertial-particle clustering in a phase-dependent way.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests periodic modulation can be used as a control knob to tune mixing and particle organization in jets without major changes to the mean flow.
method: Hot-wire anemometry measured carrier-flow turbulence in a periodically forced planar jet.
High-speed particle imaging tracked dilute inertial droplets.
Voronoi tessellations quantified preferential concentration and its variation over the forcing cycle.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two Reynolds numbers (~4950 and ~9900), forcing reduced the integral scale by up to 40% and changed clustering by 21–49% of its cycle mean, while the mean-flow evolution stayed nearly unchanged.
infographic.watch_item: The control effect is strongly phase dependent, so conclusions based on cycle-averaged quantities can miss large instantaneous changes in clustering and dissipation.
infographic.paper_title: Preferential concentration in a periodically forced particle-laden turbulent planar jet

title: Versatile two-layer model for thermohydraulic prediction of microchannel heat sinks
authors: Chih-Hsiang Chen, Kentaro Yaji
abstract: Three-dimensional conjugate heat-transfer simulations provide detailed predictions for microchannel heat sinks but can be computationally demanding when many geometries and operating conditions are evaluated. This study develops a versatile two-layer model (VTLM) that reduces the three-dimensional problem to two coupled two-dimensional fields while retaining the in-plane geometry of the flow passages and fins. Effects associated with the unresolved channel-height direction are incorporated through hydraulic and thermal closures that account for wall friction and the fluid- and fin-side contributions to interlayer heat transfer. The closures are evaluated from the representative channel geometry, flow-development condition, and fin configuration. The VTLM was assessed against three-dimensional reference models across broad ranges of channel aspect ratios and operating conditions, including uniform and nonuniform fin arrangements. Compared with the existing two-layer models, the VTLM showed improved overall agreement with the three-dimensional reference results. The results showed that prediction accuracy was governed mainly by the flow-development condition and channel aspect ratio, from which a conservative screening guideline was proposed for the examined straight-channel configurations. The assessment of finned expansion--contraction channels further supported the applicability of the VTLM to the investigated passages with abrupt width changes. Overall, the VTLM provides a reduced-dimensional framework for thermohydraulic analysis across the range of microchannel heat-sink configurations examined in this study without explicitly resolving the channel-height direction.

infographic.key_insight: A versatile two-layer model (VTLM) can replace full 3D microchannel heat-sink simulations with coupled 2D fields while still capturing key thermohydraulic effects.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a faster design tool for screening many microchannel geometries and operating conditions without explicitly resolving the channel-height direction.
method: Maps the 3D conjugate heat-transfer problem to two coupled 2D fields.
Uses hydraulic and thermal closure relations to represent wall friction and interlayer heat transfer.
Calibrates closures from representative channel geometry, flow-development state, and fin configuration.
infographic.evidence_signal: The VTLM was evaluated against 3D reference models over broad ranges of channel aspect ratio, operating condition, and fin arrangement, and it showed improved agreement over prior two-layer models.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends strongly on flow-development condition and channel aspect ratio, so the conservative screening guideline should be checked before using the model outside the examined configurations.
infographic.paper_title: Versatile two-layer model for thermohydraulic prediction of microchannel heat sinks
